                                    PROJECT NO. 58482

 LARGE LOAD DEMAND                              §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
                                                §
 MANAGEMENT SERVICE                             §                   OF TEXAS


             COMMENTS OF THE TEXAS ENERGY BUYERS ALLIANCE

                                     I.​   INTRODUCTION

        The Texas Energy Buyers Alliance (TEBA) represents the collective voice of more than

200 companies, representing some of the state’s largest employers and energy customers. In

total, TEBA members represent more than $36 trillion in market capitalization and hundreds of

thousands of employees in Texas. Our organization is focused on helping to shape Texas’

electricity market redesign in ways that propel Texas’ economy forward, lower power bills for all

energy customers, create jobs, spur innovation, strengthen the ERCOT grid, and extend Texas’

energy leadership through the energy transition and for generations to come.



     II.​   RESPONSES TO COMMISSION STAFF’S QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT



        1. Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity

representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is

subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management Service

(LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available but not

ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be compensated some

percentage of the market clearing price for the large load customer' s availability to reduce

demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate payment to the

large load customer for their availability during the LLDMS obligation period?
        No, a large load customer should not be compensated a percentage of the market clearing

price because this would result in a double payment. An important concept to understand when

answering this question is the block-and-index product, a common product type in the

competitive retail market that is often mirrored by electric cooperatives. A block-plus-index

product involves the retailer buying a flat or shaped block of power for the customer for a fixed

price per megawatt-hour. Any consumption above the block is charged at the real time price plus

an adder, and any consumption below the block is paid to the customer at the real time price

minus the adder. Large commercial and industrial consumers leverage when buying power to

buy lower cost energy in ERCOT. When prices are high and scarcity events are triggered,

customers with a flexible index have the opportunity to profit, compared to customers with larger

blocks that have already secured their prices. Avoiding high prices with flexibility significantly

lowers the average cost for the customer.

       If this product awards customers for being available in a scarcity situation, that customer

could be getting paid twice: once for the retail contract it’s selected, and then again through the

LLDMS product. A customer who does not have the built-in incentive made that choice through

the contract that they structured, and it is not a gap that ERCOT needs to cover through an

availability payment.

       There’s no need to replicate the retail market through regulatory mechanisms.



       2. Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a

calendar year. What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

       The budget per calendar year should be based on the value of lost load cost above the

real-time market price multiplied by the estimated quantity projected procured on an annual
 basis. Bids in the program will be based on the customer’s own value of loss load (“VOLL”),

which should be submitted through a bid.

       In the case that the $54 million budget is advanced, TEBA would like to respectfully

request information on how this value was determined. This value of $54 million seems

relatively arbitrary, and if this Commission moves forward with this ceiling, it’s necessary to

provide the calculation methodology and input factors that determined this amount.



       3. What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and

how far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

       Regarding the second part of this question, we believe ERCOT should use a laddered

forward procurement schedule that begins two years in advance. Under this framework, we

propose that ERCOT procure half of what is needed two years in advance, and the other half one

year in advance. Using 2028 as an example, ERCOT would procure 50% of the product through

an auction in 2026, and then hold another auction in 2027 to procure the second half. The first

year would be an exception to this rule, as 100% of the LLDMS would need to be procured for

the upcoming year.

       Spreading procurement across different time frames creates a more competitive

framework for buyers. Using the 2028 example, if a load is bidding in the 2026 auction, it cannot

be too aggressive with its bids in this first auction because it knows ERCOT will be back for the

remaining 50% in 2027, where another bidder can undercut them in the next auction.



       4. Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If

so, what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?
        No, ERCOT should not be allowed to deploy this service for transmission emergencies, it

should be reserved for capacity shortages tied to extreme weather only. Senate Bill 6 does not

direct that this service to be deployed for transmission emergencies, and the Commission should

not extend SB6’s language past what it directs. Additionally, extending LLDMS to cover

transmission emergencies would blur the lines between transmission emergencies and capacity

emergencies, making it more difficult for customers to understand what they should be prepared

for. TEBA recommends that the PUCT evaluate other methods and technologies specifically

suited to manage transmission constraints.

       Avoiding transmission emergencies gives far too much authority to ERCOT to curtail

loads based on their judgement, whereas capacity shortages are well-understood.



         III.​   COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION LANGUAGE

​      In addition to our response to Commission staff’s questions, we also submit the following

feedback and considerations related to the language used throughout the Proposal for

Publication. Our comments and proposed redlines will be discussed following the same

organization as the proposed rule.



Proposed Revision to §25.521(a)(1)

       The opening subsection in this rulemaking directs ERCOT to work with the TDSPs to

establish a program with TDSPs for firm load shed of large loads during emergency conditions.

It’s critical that the conditions of an emergency are clearly defined in an attempt to standardize

this process and the circumstances under which it would occur across the state. This process
 should additionally be developed with stakeholders to ensure emergency conditions are clearly

communicated and can be anticipated by large energy consumers that will be impacted.

Proposed Redline to §25.521(a)(1)

       (1)​    ERCOT must ensure that each electric cooperative, transmission and distribution

       utility, and municipally owned utility serving a transmission-voltage customer develops a

       protocol, including the installation of any necessary equipment or technology before the

       customer is interconnected, to allow the load to be curtailed during firm load shed.

       ERCOT must clearly define the conditions which would elicit a firm load shed before the

       utilities develop their firm load shed protocols. These conditions must be established in

       compliance with the existing stakeholder process. This subsection applies to a load

       interconnected after December 31,2025, that is not:



Proposed Rule §25.521(b)(1)

       Proposed subsection (b)(1) defines extreme weather events. We propose revising the

definition of emergency weather event to provide more specific language “Significant risk using

a quantitative methodology defined in the ERCOT protocols.” We are concerned that the current

definition is too broad and creates room to be interpreted in a flexible manner or to vary

depending on who is making the decision. It’s important to the success of the LLDMS program

that extreme weather events that would trigger this service are consistently defined, therefore we

propose that a quantitative methodology be developed to assess a number of weather factors to

determine what an extreme weather event would be. We request that guardrails are created that

clearly outline the methodology to reach this point.

Proposed Redline to §25.521(b)(1)
         (1)​    Extreme weather condition -- A weather condition that creates a significant risk

        for an energy emergency alert (EEA) event, determined using a quantitative methodology

        that is determined in the ERCOT protocols.



Proposed Rule §25.521(d)(3)(B)(v)

        We recommend revising §25.521(d)(3)(B)(v). As drafted, the provision requires ERCOT

to reject any offer greater than $5,000 per megawatt hour. We believe the threshold should work

in the opposite direction – a large load customer willing to accept $5,000 per megawatt hour or

less to curtail is a customer whose Value of Loss Load (“VOLL”) is at or below ERCOT’s own

real-time energy price cap.

        Consider a customer that has a value of lost load at $20,000 per MWh – this customer has

no incentive to curtail in a $5,000 price cap market unless they are forced to. A targeted contract

under this program could make that curtailment voluntary and economic if the payment was for

the delta of $15,000 per megawatt-hour. This payment is what actually changes the custom’s

behavior.

        For this reason, accepting offers from these customers with a value of lost load below

$5,000 per MWh produces no incremental reliability benefit, but instead just pays customers to

do what the energy market already encourages them to do.

        With this in mind, it may be necessary to target customers with the lowest values of lost

load that are still above $5,000 to minimize the cost of this program and still provide incremental

reliability benefit. A customer with a $6,000 VOLL would only require a $1,000 delta payment

to make curtailing economic. This approach could result in a lower overall program costs while

still providing the additional reliability benefit.
        Overall, we emphasize that the LLDMS should be designed to target customers with

VOLL that are above the offer cap that would not be responsive to high energy prices during

periods of scarcity, not exclude them. We recommend that the Commission instead reject offers

at or below $5,000 so that the program targets loads with a high VOLL. Related, we recommend

that the overall program cost and budget be reconsidered in this framework.

Proposed Redline §25.521(d)(1)

       (B)​    Rejection. ERCOT must reject an offer that is:

               (v)​    less greater than $5,000 per megawatt hour.



Proposed Rule §25.521(e)

       ERCOT should explicitly define the communication pathways used to recall a

curtailment, so that these messages can be executed smoothly and reliably once emergency

conditions arise. We further request that ERCOT be required to communicate the anticipated

length of the event, even if it is just an estimate. Finally, ERCOT should be required to make

every reasonable effort to recall curtailed loads as soon as practical.

Proposed Redlines §25.521(e)

       (3)​    When deployed by ERCOT, a large load customer must deploy consistent with its

       obligations and must remain deployed:

               (A)​    for the duration of the EEA event; or

               (B)​    until the large load customer can be recalled safely, as determined and

               communicated by ERCOT leveraging a communication method outlined in the

               ERCOT protocols.
                (C)​    ERCOT must provide a time estimate at the time of curtailment that the

               event is estimated to last.

​      (4)​    ERCOT must recall the curtailed load as soon as practical.



Proposed Rule §25.521(f)(1):

       Regarding settlements, we recommend that language be edited to give ERCOT the

opportunity to settle more than monthly. The rule should not inhibit ERCOT from settling more

than monthly if they decide it’s more credit-efficient to settle more frequently.

       We additionally recommend that subsection (C) and (D) are both struck. As drafted, it’s

unclear how the availability payment would interact with the compensation that a large load

customer is already receiving under its retail contract. We believe that paying a customer to be

ready to curtail could result in a double payment, as outlined in our responses to staff’s first

question above, by allowing them to get paid through both their contract and through this

service. For the same reason, we believe subsection (D) should also be struck.



Proposed Redline §25.521(f)(1):

       (1)​    ERCOT must pay a QSE that represents a large load customer participating in

       LLDMS as follows:

               (A)​    all payments must be based on a single clearing price; and

               (B)​    awards must be settled at least monthly after availability data is

               confirmed;

               (C)​    A QSE representing a large load customer that is not instructed by

               ERCOT to deploy but is subject to availability verification during the LLDMS
                obligation period may receive a payment based on 25% of the market clearing

               price; and

               (D)​    A QSE representing a large load customer that deploys consistent with

               ERCOT instructions during the LLDMS obligation period may receive payment

               based on 100% of the market clearing price associated with the deployed capacity.



Proposed Rule §25.521(g)(1):

       ERCOT and QSE’s should work closely with large loads to establish additional detail

under this section in relation to the circumstances that a claw back of a payment is necessary and

the degree of the clawback. We believe any scenarios that would trigger the claw back of

payments based on "noncompliance" be clearly outlined. For this reason, we request that the

Commission add definitions for compliance and noncompliance that clearly states what actions

would be in violation of compliance rules.

       We additionally believe it’s important that there is a criteria established around the

clawback amount in the case that a LLDMS obligation is not fully met. We believe this should

not be an “all or nothing” situation – For example, if a load is able to meet 90% of its obligation,

but not the final 10%, the load should still be partially awarded a portion of the financial award

for the amount that it curtailed.



Proposed Rule §25.521(h):

       Two reports, one for a detailed offer disclose list (rather than summary,) then a report on

testing and deployments performance as applicable.
        The first report following procurement of LLDMS should mirror the reporting that

happens for ERS contracts. The ERS Offer Disclosure Report includes the QSE, the submission

type, the offered and awarded capacity, the offer price, and the clearing price. We want to

emphasize the importance of including the QSE instead of the customer in this data to protect

individual consumers. Disclosing the QSE instead of the customer, as is done in the ERS Offer

Disclosure report, gives transparency to the market while protecting the names of individual

customers. In addition to these provisions, we are supportive of the suggestion of including the

duration and of deployment in this dataset.

       The second report should be a high-level summary that focuses on deployment

performance. For this, we recommend including the duration of deployment, performance during

deployment, and any recommendations to revise LLDMS. It may also be appropriate to include

the QSE in this dataset as well.

Proposed Redline §25.521(h):

       (h)​    After action reporting requirement. Not later than 60 days after an event in which

       ERCOT procures LLDMS, ERCOT must file two a reports with the commission

       detailing:.

               (1) ​   The first report should include:

                       (1A)​ the number of large load customers that submitted offers;

                       (2B)​ the number of megawatts procured;

                       (3C)​ the highest offer;

                       (4D)​ the lowest offer;

                       (5E)​ the cleared price;

                       (F)​   awarded capacity;
                         (G)​    the QSE

                (2) ​   The second report should include:

                        (6A)​ the duration of deployment, as applicable;

                        (7B)​ performance during deployment, as applicable; and

                        (8C)​ any recommendation to revise LLDMS.



Proposed Redline §25.521(i):

        We have concerns around the current language allowing ERCOT the ability to develop

additional procedures as they “find necessary” – we believe there should be guardrails around

this. As many other changes to products similar to the LLDMS, any changes to the product

should include stakeholder input and be followed by a vote by ERCOT’s Technical Advisory

Commission, Board of Directors, and approval by the Commission (as established in 2021 by

Senate Bill 2 (87R)).

        Additionally, we believe that “in consultation with Commission staff” should be struck.

This language does not need to be explicitly included, because Commission staff is already given

the authority to participate in this process.

Proposed Redline §25.521(i):

        (i)​    Implementation. ERCOT must develop, in compliance with the existing

        stakeholder process consultation with commission staff, additional procedures, including

        registration requirements for the large load customers participating in LLDMS, guides,

        technical requirements, protocols, or other standards that are consistent with this section

        and that ERCOT finds necessary to develop LLDMS.
                                     IV.​   CONCLUSION

       TEBA appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and looks forward to

continuing to work with Commission staff on this matter.



                                                   Respectfully submitted,

                                                   /s/ Bryn Baker
                                                   Bryn Baker
                                                   Texas Energy Buyers Alliance
                                                   bbaker@txenergybuyers.org

    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE TEXAS ENERGY BUYERS ALLIANCE

 ●​ A large load customer that is available but not instructed to curtail should not be

    compensated a percentage of the market clearing price because this would result in a

    double payment through the block-plus-index product.

 ●​ In place of the suggested $54 million budget, the budget per calendar year should be

    based on the value of lost load cost above the real-time market price multiplied by the

    estimated quantity projected procured on an annual basis.

 ●​ Procurement should follow a laddered forward schedule beginning two years in advance

    of each delivery year to ensure a competitive framework.

 ●​ TEBA is strongly opposed to using this service for transmission emergencies and

    emphasizes that it should be used for capacity shortages tied to extreme weather only.

    Leveraging this service for transmission emergencies gives far too much authority to

    ERCOT to curtail loads based on their judgement.

 ●​ Emergency weather events should be redefined to include a quantitative methodology to

    determine the weather emergency in order to eliminate a flexible interpretation.

 ●​ The rule should reject offers over $5,000 per MWh because this cap will not target loads

    with high VOLL and will compensate loads with a VOLL under $5,000 per MWh,

    despite that they would have already curtailed due to the high price.

 ●​ We request ERCOT be required to communicate the estimated length of curtailment and

    work to recall the curtailed load as soon as practical.

Commission add definitions for compliance and noncompliance that clearly states what actions

would be in violation of compliance rules.

       We additionally believe it's important that there is a criteria established around the

clawback amount in the case that a LLDMS obligation is not fully met. We believe this should

not be an "all or nothing" situation - For example, if a load is able to meet 90% of its obligation,

but not the final 10%, the load should still be partially awarded a portion of the financial award

for the amount that it curtailed.



Proposed Rule §25.521(h):

        Two reports, one for a detailed offer disclose list (rather than summary,) then a report on

testing and deployments performance as applicable.
        The first report following procurement of LLDMS should mirror the reporting that

happens for ERS contracts. The ERS Offer Disclosure Report includes the QSE, the submission

type, the offered and awarded capacity, the offer price, and the clearing price. We want to

emphasize the importance of including the QSE instead of the customer in this data to protect

individual consumers. Disclosing the QSE instead of the customer, as is done in the ERS Offer

Disclosure report, gives transparency to the market while protecting the names of individual

customers. In addition to these provisions, we are supportive of the suggestion of including the

duration and of deployment in this dataset.

       The second report should be a high-level summary that focuses on deployment

performance. For this, we recommend including the duration of deployment, performance during

deployment, and any recommendations to revise LLDMS. It may also be appropriate to include

the QSE in this dataset as well.

     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE TEXAS ENERGY BUYERS ALLIANCE

 •   A large load customer that is available but not instructed to curtail should not be

     compensated a percentage of the market clearing price because this would result in a

     double payment through the block-plus-index product.

 •   In place of the suggested $54 million budget, the budget per calendar year should be

     based on the value of lost load cost above the real-time market price multiplied by the

     estimated quantity projected procured on an annual basis.

 •   Procurement should follow a laddered forward schedule beginning two years in advance

     of each delivery year to ensure a competitive framework.

 •   TEBA is strongly opposed to using this service for transmission emergencies and

     emphasizes that it should be used for capacity shortages tied to extreme weather only.

     Leveraging this service for transmission emergencies gives far too much authority to

     ERCOT to curtail loads based on their judgement.

 •   Emergency weather events should be redefined to include a quantitative methodology to

     determine the weather emergency in order to eliminate a flexible interpretation.

 •   The rule should reject offers over $5,000 per MWh because this cap will not target loads

     with high VOLL and will compensate loads with a VOLL under $5,000 per MWh,

     despite that they would have already curtailed due to the high price.

 •   We request ERCOT be required to communicate the estimated length of curtailment and

     work to recall the curtailed load as soon as practical.
